speakeroldname: Mr. F. Oberle (Prince George-Peace River) moved:
speechtext:
That this House regards the Government's failure to take action to encourage the development of Canada's resource industries and ensure their competitiveness in world markets as a betrayal of all Canadians whose standard of living depends upon the resource sector of Canada's economy and calls upon the Government to bring an end to the nationalization of Canadian resource industries which has discouraged investment in Canada; introduce tax incentives to restore competitive advantage and stimulate resource production and further processing in Canada; initiate a program of incentives for research and development; and incentives for marketing activities of Canadian industries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am certain that the House will not be surprised that we should have chosen to put aside a day in the busy life of Parliament to discuss the state of our primary resource sector, and therefore the economy in general. Naturally we would have preferred to discuss issues so vital to the well-being of our entire nation and her people in connection with any Government initiatives.
Despite our strong urgings here in the House and the danger signals which we are receiving from the industry, the unions, and the scientific community associated with it, and from the investment communities that invest in the resource sector, this Government sticks stubbornly to a deliberate policy of indifference and neglect. This Government sees our primary resources such as trees and minerals as artesian fountains of wealth which will flow uninterruptedly to be tapped and sapped at every stage without regard to the health of the resource itself or the industries that are sustained by it. It makes no difference whether we talk of our forests which could be, with reasonable care, renewable, or the minerals which we extract and refine and which are such an important part of our commerce and trade. This Government's only interest is what these industries can be made to contribute to satisfy the monstrous appetite for public revenues to support a spending spree over which no one any longer has any control.
My colleagues will, in the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, tell you of some of the horror stories which are the result of 15 years of Liberal mismanagement. We will speak of the imminent crisis facing our resource sector. We will also point out the great opportunities that we have missed in the past and
will surely miss in the future if we fail to act responsibly and decisively to arrest the disease which has been inflicted on private sector industries in general and the resource sector in our economy in particular.
I share the view of many economists who say that Canada could hardly survive as an important and viable trading nation without its resource wealth, if for no other reason than the fact that the volume and potential for growth of one's industrial production is, in the main, limited by the size of one's markets. All of us want to expand our secondary manufacturing capacities and our markets for such products through trade with foreign countries. But it is in the resource sectors wherein lies our natural strength and advantage. It is our resource industries which provide the foundation for the economic structure which permits us to compete in a significant way in world markets. It is our resource sector which is the source of our economic well-being, our prosperity, and social contentment.
Permit me, in the few minutes that 1 have to speak on the motion standing in my name, to give a profile of just two of our more important resource industries, mining and forestry. I think I might best be able to describe the importance of those two industries by comparing our total economic structure to the trunk of a tree which supports its branches and its leaves through a network of roots through which flow its life-supporting juices.
There are now more than 350 small and not so small communities throughout our country, from the Great Lakes to the Arctic Ocean, which depend almost entirely on one or the other of these two industries I have mentioned. These communities are at the end of the root structure or network, generating wealth and nourishment which sustains the life at the end of the branch.
Fifteen per cent of our country's entire work force is either directly or indirectly engaged in the forest and mining sectors. In better times these two industries have generated directly close to $40 billion of industrial product, $25 billion of which is earned from trade in foreign markets throughout the world. The mining sector alone accounts for over 50 per cent of all our rail freight volume, with crude minerals making up 44 per cent and fabricated minerals 9 per cent of all the railways' revenue freight handled. Forty-one per cent of all goods shipped through the St. Lawrence Seaway originate from the end of one of the root canals, from a quarry, sandpit, mine smelter or refinery, a sawmill, pulpmill or logging camps some place in mid-Canada or the North.
It is the activities of the miners and the loggers which sustain some form of economic life in over 60 per cent of our

entire geography. The further the roots have been extended, the healthier and stronger our tree has become.
But something has gone terribly wrong. The engine which pumps the vital juices through the trunk is working at only 50 per cent capacity. On the mineral side, half of our mines are shut down or have drastically reduced production. The Government says that it is just another cyclical problem, the result of a world-wide recession in the economy, and is something we will just have to wait out. Of course, that is true to some extent but it would be extremely dangerous to ignore a number of trends and factors which will undoubtedly have a profound effect on the timing and rate or extent to which our mining industry can recover from this deep valley of a cyclical curve.
First, it must be obvious by now to even the most casual observer that there is a fundamental shift of resource-based industrial production toward the developing world. Industrial countries in Europe and Japan, even ourselves and the Americans, are making massive investments in the resource sectors of many developing countries. We see it as our contribution or form of development aid or assistance. But in the case of our industrial competitors from Europe and Japan, it also has the purpose of adding to the supply of raw materials to achieve greater and more diversified access to natural resources and, through it all, to create keener price competition. As well, the World Bank is very active in this field. While all this activity may produce significant benefits to the target countries and the industrial countries which make the investments, it spells bad news for Canada.
A second, equally important factor is the substitution in the manufacturing process of certain base minerals for new materials and a general impact of a new technological revolution of which we are becoming the beneficiaries, or perhaps the victims, at an extremely rapid pace. For instance, the same tonne of coal that it used to take to produce 90 miles of copper wire now turns out 80,000 miles of fibre cable capable of delivering 100 times more impulses. Or an automobile which used to weigh 5,000 pounds ten years ago now weighs only
3,000	pounds. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, it would take unprecedented growth in world markets to generate the kind of demand for our base metals needed to restore our mining sector to its original health.
Finally, there is another factor more of a home made kind which will undoubtedly delay the recovery of our industry and therefore the economy generally. That has to do with the unreasonably heavy and crushing tax burden and economic rent structure which all levels of government have loaded on the shoulders of the resource sectors in recent years, a burden out of all proportion to any return the industry has achieved from its investment.
There have been unconscionable increases of certain so called non-profit taxes, such as property tax, fuel taxes and so on. In some cases these charges have increased by over 100 per cent in one year, diminishing the efforts the industry has been making in cutting costs and increasing productivity.
The Mining Association of Canada in its submission to this year's conference of resource ministers gave a number of examples to illustrate this point. Let me quote:
In British Columbia and in the period 1980-1982, costs to the industry have increased by $118.5 million in direct payments arising from a very large number of actions by Government, both federal and provincial, on several fronts. This represents a 105 per cent increase in only two years. For 1983 it is anticipated that further substantial increases have occurred. More specifically, we have evidence to show that in the past 12 years, two large mining operations in British Columbia have seen their property, fuel, water, provincial and municipal taxes escalate from $4 million to $35 million.
In Quebec, salary and fringe benefits, which in 1980 represented 32.2 per cent of the average value per tonne of ore, increased in 1982 to 38.8 per cent of this average value, representing a 20.5 per cent increase. On the other hand, the cost of social policies, indirect taxes and electrical power, which in 1980 represented 9.67 per cent of the average value per tonne of ore, reached a percentage of 15.62 in 1982, i.e., an increase of 61 per cent during the period. So together, the cost of all these items measured, on the average value per tonne of ore, went from 41.9 per cent in 1980 to 54.3 per cent in 1982.
In Alberta, over the past Five years mining companies have experienced percentage increases of over 100 per cent for fuels, 80 per cent for electric power, 75 per cent for freight costs, 60 per cent for property taxes, 85 per cent for provincial health care premiums, 62 per cent for unemployment insurance, and 41 per cent for pension contributions.
Very similar increases could be documented in every province or territory across Canada where mining is carried on. To add to all that, we keep inventing ever more stringent rules with respect to environmental safeguards, health, safety and standards of social amenities in the mining and logging communities.
Now, Sir, you will find me among the very last to suggest that some of the standards which we have all worked hard to achieve should be sacrificed to assure the future health of the resource sector. But it is now painfully obvious to everyone that the industries alone are no longer able to bear all the costs related to these laudable social objectives. We have simply strapped the industry too tight. We are depriving it of its competitive edge and rendering ourselves extremely vulnerable and unprepared to meet the new challenges and forces which have distorted the conventional rules of trade in market places of the world.
Our new competitors, as you know, Mr. Speaker, may not play by the same rules or by what we would consider conventional rules. They are in the main state-owned enterprises, their prime objective, understandably perhaps, being foreign exchange earnings and jobs. Their plants will be heavily subsidized from funds to which we ourselves are contributing. It is as if we are all too eager to finance our own demise.
Well, Sir, one might ask how is the Government on the other side of the House reacting to these worrisome trends? Sureiy it must have the same information we have. To some of us it appears as if its answer to our dilemma is to succumb to the rule changes and attempt to compete on an equal basis with the new players in the developing world and the not so new players in the socialist world. It appears as if it sees states ownership, or at least a very advanced form of state control, in our own country's economy as the only way to survive this onslaught.
November 21, 1983

In a sense we have advanced some way toward that goal. The justification for Petro-Canada, for instance, was to provide us with a window on the world and permit us to trade with countries that refused to deal with the private sector. Our tax laws are designed to permit our companies barely to cover their costs of capital and operation and leave no room for modernization and technological innovation.
"Not to worry," says the Government, "after all have we not given you grants to modernize or subsidies for labour costs when that became your problem?" That may be true, but do you believe, Sir, that this is the kind of climate to which either our own or foreign investors feel attracted? That must be a worry, unless we either believe the Government can create money out of thin air or we assume that after necessary adjustments to our economy have been perfected we might ourselves become eligible some day for loans and gifts from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
What happens if one falls out of favour with the Government on which one has to rely for grants when things get tough, or what happens if it is too late before the bureaucrats in Ottawa get around to a particular problem? The forest industry is a case in point. It is suffering not only from all the pains of the recession and the fact that we have not permitted the industry to build and maintain its own capital resources to ride out the storm, but because we have also neglected to assure that our forests are replenished to provide our mills in the future with the necessary feedstock on the basis of a sustained yield. All of a sudden we have come to realize that we have been mining our forests for the last 200 years instead of farming them and that nature alone is no longer able to replenish itself in sufficient time to meet our demand.
For some mills and towns in mid-Canada, coming to grips with this realization is too late. No matter how many grants the Government might make to bail out a troubled company, we will shortly experience timber shortages in most areas and regions of the country, causing lay-offs and shutdowns not only of mills but of whole towns and regions, because it takes 60 years to grow a tree and sometimes much longer, depending upon the climate and other factors.
1 have little doubt that had it been the responsibility of the private sector to manage the resource, either through direct ownership or long-term tenure, we would not find ourselves in this fix today. The United States, where 60 per cent of the forest land is privately owned and managed, provides us with an interesting model for comparison.
To sum up, we see difficult times ahead for our resource industries and therefore for our economic wellbeing. Any prospects for recovery and new growth are admittedly, as 1 pointed out, influenced by factors and trends over which we have little control. However, much of the pain we must suffer during the recovery period is self-afflicted and can be cured only by ourselves, even though some of the larger corporations and their sector organizations still refuse to speak out in defence of the system from which they have grown, I suppose for fear that the Government might not think kindly of them

at their time of need. Some do speak out and, more important, the average Canadian has become weary of the dream of a just society which our centrally-structured and planned economy was to deliver, a dream which for some has turned into a nightmare. Canadians now understand that state planners are not very good in creating new wealth and that Government cannot distribute wealth which has not first been created by someone.
It is true that we have built for ourselves a very sophisticated socio-economic structure, one which is still the envy of most of the world and indeed one which can feed on itself for a short period of time. However, like the maple tree that has been tapped too deeply, it will eventually die, and like any tree that has been cut off from its roots, it will rot and decay.

We draw our confidence for not only bright but exciting future prospects for economic growth and prosperity from the confidence Canadians are expressing in my Party's ability to recapture the promise which inspired earlier generations of Canadians, the promise of a just reward for individual effort and free enterprise. Most assuredly if we should manage once again to set this spirit free, we shall have no trouble meeting and beating whatever our new competition will throw at us in world markets.
I thank the House for giving us this day to state the case and for preparing Canadians for the challenge ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are Hon. Members rising to ask questions or make brief comments on the remarks of the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle)? If not, the Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to rise today to address what has to be one of the most critical problems facing our country. I thank the Hon. Member for bringing forward this motion which in part reads:
That this House regards the Government's failure to take action to encourage the development of Canada's resource industries and ensure their competitiveness in world markets as a betrayal of all Canadians whose standard of living depends upon the resource sector of Canada's economy-
While the motion goes on to refer to a number of other interesting and important matters, the essence of the motion is presented in those few words. Indeed, it is a betrayal of many Canadians.
1 want to focus my remarks this morning on one of our most critical resource industries, the forest industry of Canada. One could comment, as the previous speaker did, on the mining industry, the fishing industry and all the resource sectors. By and large the critical comments would be appropriate in terms of how not only the federal Government but the provincial Governments, and in many cases industry itself, have failed to live up to the challenges of the present time.
I want to focus my remarks today on the forest industry. This industry has by and large been overlooked by Canadians.

November 21, 1983
Supply
We have now been in session in excess of 600 days, the longest session of Parliament in Canadian history. We have managed as a result of an Opposition initiative to discuss forestry for a single day.
When you consider the importance of the forest industry and the impact which the forest industry has on the balance of payments in this country, Mr. Speaker, there is more economic impact in terms of our country's trade balance than the entire agriculture industry, mining industry, fishing industry and auto industry combined. That is the immensity of this one industry that we are discussing today. It is of incredible importance.
If you look closely at the statistics, you find that 1.3 million Canadians are involved in one way or another with the forest industry in terms of their jobs. In other words, they are employed either in a direct way or in an indirect way with the forest industry. It involves 1,300,000 Canadians. There are
5,000	forest companies spread from one end of the country to the other. Three hundred communities depend 100 per cent on the forest industry. We are talking about an industry of immense proportions.
1 believe it is fair to say that the problem associated with the forest industry has not been clearly understood by many Canadians. A number who have watched or who live close to the industry have known for many years that it is in a virtual crisis situation. I would say there is a national emergency in Canada today as it touches on that critical resource industry, the forest industry of Canada.
We can look back, however, to a politician from 1871, none other than John A. Macdonald himself, who at that time said that we are recklessly destroying the timber of Canada and there is scarcely a possibility of replacing it. Here we are, more than 100 years later, Mr. Speaker, and we are saying that same thing today in the House of Commons. We are saying that we are seeing the erosion of the most critical industry in the country in terms of the balance of payments and employability of Canadians, and we are seeing the erosion of that industry in every single Province.
When we consider that last year we harvested approximately 800,000 hectares of forest land, it is interesting to note that we managed to replace 25 per cent of that in terms of reforestation. Only 25 per cent of the most critical resource in the country was replanted, albeit additional hectares were replanted naturally. However, there is nothing to say but that the shortfall in reforestation in the country is absolutely astounding.
I would like to focus on a couple of points that simply indicate the critical nature of the problems facing us today. I suppose it is not surprising that Canadians have not been alert to the nature of this problem. After all, 95 per cent of Canadians are urban dwellers and live in big cities like Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Regina and Hamilton. We do not come into contact with the forests of Canada on a
regular basis, so naturally many of us are a little out of tune with the realities out there.
However, Mr. Speaker, if you ask any single individual in the logging sector, the lumber sector, the plywood sector, the pulp and paper sector, the shake sector or any other sector of the forest industry, they will tell you that the industry is in serious trouble today. Every professional organization in the country related to the forest industry will say the same thing. As a matter of fact, 1 remember a number of presentations in the last three years from professional foresters to Members of Parliament on an individual basis, a caucus basis and a professional basis. Those organizations have said that this industry is in serious trouble and that we must do something about it not next year, not next decade, but immediately.
What do we do, Mr. Speaker? Do we take action? Does the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) who is responsible for forestry call for special debates in the House of Commons? Does he call for extraordinary steps to be taken? 1 do not hear a great deal from him, but to give the Minister credit where credit is due, I will say that he has indicated an interest in this area and has recognized some concerns. Perhaps he is having difficulty with some of his Cabinet colleagues when trying to put his money where his mouth is when identifying the problems and their solutions in the forest industry.
I would like to quote from a number of people I feel are representative of respectable forest voices. Jack Walters, the director of the UBC research forest on the West Coast, had this to say recently: "Our forests are in a shambles. It is a tragedy of the first dimension." This is a professional forester speaking out in an attempt to communicate to the powers that be and particularly to the politicians both provincial and federal, that we have a serious problem. Mr. Michael Innes, the manager of forestry for Abitibi Price, the world's largest producer of newsprint, said: "We are gradually running out of wood." He is saying that we are gradually running out of merchantable timber in the country and that we must now transport the product in many cases hundreds and hundreds of miles from the forest to the processing plants. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we are failing to replant those forests which stand right in front of the processing facilities.
The forest industry's advisory committee to the Government, Mr. Speaker, recently made a plea for more financial assistance to this troubled industry. The Science Council of Canada targeted the problem clearly, I believe, when it said that 6,000 square miles of forest land is destroyed or wasted each year. The IWA said that we are running out of merchantable timber, that the industry is virtually at a crossroads and that it will either fail or succeed, depending upon the initiative taken by governments and industry. The Quebec and Ontario furniture manufacturers recently brought to our attention that they are now required to import maple logs from the United States because sufficient supplies of maple do not exist here in Canada for use by the Canadian furniture industry.
I would like to go on and relate to you, Mr. Speaker, two or three of the problems that were brought to our attention as parliamentarians and legislators by the Association of B.C.

Professional Foresters. That association has brought to our attention the fact that more than 800,000 hectares are harvested annually in our country but less than 25 per cent are planted or seeded. In British Columbia, more than a million hectares heed reforestation and British Columbia is adding
20,000	to 50,000 hectares annually to this problem. Yet the B.C. Ministry of Forests recently had budget cuts in this area which will simply exacerbate the problem.
The number of person-years available to research in the Canadian Forestry Service has declined by more than 50 per cent since 1968. We are talking about an industry in which research and development has never been more needed and demanded than today. Yet the professional foresters tell us that money for research and development in the Canadian Forestry Service has declined by more than 50 per cent since 1968. Increased research is required in almost all phases of forestry management.
The association goes on to say that current spending on silviculture by ail parties, including industry and provincial and federal Governments alike, amounts to about $240 million a year. This is less than 1 per cent of the total value of the annual forest production in the country; we are reinvesting less than 1 per cent of its total value in that critical resource. We can look at some of our competitors in western Europe. For instance, Sweden spends between $700 million and $1 billion annually as compared to our expenditure of $240 million. That is the kind of husbandry with which our competitors are treating their forests in terms of silviculture, reforestation, spacing, thinning, road building, fire prevention and disease prevention. They are spending up to $1 billion annually compared to our paltry expenditure of $240 million. If that does not spell doom for this industry in the long run, Mr. Speaker, then I do not know what does.
The Canadian Forestry Service is a part of Environment Canada and $69.4 million was allocated to the Canadian Forest Service. Within the same Ministry, $146 million was budgeted for the Atmospheric Environment Service and $275 million was allocated for Parks Canada. The Professional Association of Foresters from British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, goes on to say that it is a national disgrace that the federal Government spends twice as much money monitoring weather as it does on our forest industry. That is not to suggest that any cutbacks should occur in weather and climate monitoring, Mr. Speaker, but 1 think that when these people put their professional careers before the public for scrutiny by standing up and saying that this is a national disgrace, we as Members of Parliament cannot stand idly by and say: "Well, 1 suppose that is just more rhetoric about this issue". The people who are most knowledgeable about the state of the forestry industry in Canada are calling the present situation a national disaster.
The association goes on to speak, Mr. Speaker, about a problem in the Province of British Columbia which is, of course, the major forest producer in the country and one of the major areas in terms of available merchantable timber. The association indicates that forestry is the largest economic activity in B.C. It generates more direct and indirect Govern-

ment revenues and employment than any other sector by far. This wealth comes from forests which are 95 per cent owned by the people of the Province yet less than 1 per cent of the new provincial budget in British Columbia is set aside for reforestation, a significant drop from last year. Can you imagine anything more akin to committing economic hara-kiri, Mr. Speaker, than spending less than ever before on reforestation at a time when the need and the demand is so great?
The association indicates that no money has been allocated this year for improving this resource, and that includes money needed for thinning, refertilization of young forests and particularly for dealing with the 29,000 square kilometers of forest land that sits idle in British Columbia. This is a critical statement, Mr. Speaker. If reforested, these lands could produce more than six million cubic metres of wood annually, and up to 20,000 new permanent jobs in the Province of British Columbia. It further states that more than 40 per cent of the funding was cut for forest protection activities. We have, it is said, more than a million hectares of idle land in the Province of British Columbia which requires treatment to return it to a new forest. At the backlog planting rate of this new plan of the provincial Government, it will take that Government 50 years to reforest these areas. 1 believe there is no question but that we are at a crossroads with Canada's number one industry.
The situation in which we find ourselves in terms of provincial governments, the federal Government, as well as a good part of the industry, is a crisis situation. Fast year the forest companies in Canada lost $500 million, but they were anticipating an improved situation for this year. However, I believe any Hon. Member of Parliament who comes from a forest related area will know that things have not turned around, that the pulp and paper industry is in a very tough situation and that the lumber industry is simply struggling to survive. Most of us with saw mills in our riding will know that they have closed, or shifts have been laid off in the last two or three weeks. That would indicate what is coming down the pipe in the months ahead.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we have an ideal opportunity now as parliamentarians to take a positive step and show that, yes, we are concerned and are prepared to do something about it. We must recognize that we have created an evergreen ghetto in this country. What was once a dynamic, thriving community is now decaying. There is now a sense of despair and a demoralization in the ranks. We are turning our backs on that part of our community. However, the evergreen ghetto can be turned around with some positive leadership and initiatives. We have heard speakers today indicate what some of those actions should be. 1 wonder, Mr. Speaker, if you would entertain a call for unanimous consent of the House to present a motion asking the Minister of the Environment, who is responsible for forestry, to call a meeting of all provincial ministers of forestry early in the new year, to have as the number one agenda item the formation of a federal ministry of forestry. speechtext: Would the Hon. Member care to present the Chair with a copy of the motion he has in mind?

Mr. Speaker, if I may say for clarification, realizing that at this point to present a motion would be presumptuous on my part, I am simply asking for unanimous consent of the House to enable me to present such a motion. The motion would in fact urge the Minister of the Environment to call a meeting of provincial ministers of forestry and the number one item on their agenda would be the formation of a federal ministry of forestry. I am asking for unanimous consent.

I appreciate your patience on this issue, Mr. Speaker, and also the patience of Hon. Members. Not feeling that a motion to amend the motion before us may be in order, 1 was, first of all, seeking unanimous consent of the House through you, Mr. Speaker, to allow me to put such a motion.

I certainly will, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate your patience. Mr. Speaker, on the motion today and the remarks made by the Hon. Member, I wonder, based on the fact that he made a very strong plea and placed a very strong thrust on the subject, whether he has any comments to enlighten the House with respect to any recommendations he would make in light of the difficult situation of the variation in value of money in various countries where we have to sell our products, the question of competitiveness with other countries south of the border, the American pulp and paper industry? Would the Hon. Member tell us exactly what he would put forward, not in terms of the motion brought forward today by his Party, but what firm recommendations can he make with respect to the difficulties with which this particular industry is faced today? Could he tell us something about that?

I certainly would like to respond to the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker. When it comes to suggestions as to what may be done to improve the situation in the forest industry, I would like to focus, perhaps, on one aspect, and that is the whole matter of what might be termed "reforestation". 1 can recall at least seven presentations which various organizations related to the forest industry have made to Members of Parliament in the past 12 months. They dealt with such recommendations as site preparation; burning or ploughing for reforestation; planting trees or seeding areas, using genetically improved seed or planting stock; choosing the best species for a site; thinning and spacing trees for optimum growth; pruning and fertilization when needed; reducing losses through fire, insect and disease; improved utilization of our present resource during logging; concentrating our efforts on the best reserved forest areas for the time necessary to grow the crop, and so on. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the need to reforest is accepted as a reality by all who are sensitive to the forest industry.
November 21, 1983

This type of "Government spending" I believe is a misnomer and ought to be called "Government investment". After all, what we are doing is investing in a resource which will presumably pay back to the Government both in terms of royalties and personal and corporate income taxes in the years ahead. Considering that this investment made now will result in returns to the Government in the years ahead, it has to be done now, and it will never be done cheaper. The need for employing people in this particular activity has never been greater. Instantly, once the decision is made to embark on a massive initiative of reforestation in all parts of Canada, it will literally provide tens of thousands of jobs for Canadians in every Province and territory. At a time when the need for job creation in a meaningful sense is so acute, surely a step in this direction has to be one of the most appropriate the federal Government could initiate at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not disagree with that aspect. I underline as well the importance of reforestation. Indeed, in my home Province of New Brunswick we have to this date accomplished a great deal in reforestation through various companies such as the Irving Group, International Paper and others.
Specifically, Mr. Speaker, taking the term used in the Hon. Member's motion with respect to competitiveness, I was asking what concrete proposals does the Hon. Member have regarding the economics of the day, the problems we have with selling these products? We have the problems of competitiveness, variations in the value of the pound and the dollar and other currencies used by countries we trade with. What does the Hon. Member have to tell the House about concrete proposals and recommendations he would make to the Government or industry to try to alleviate this serious problem he has stressed so forcefully in his speech today?

Mr. Speaker, let me identify three or four things 1 think would be appropriate, particularly when it comes to the competitiveness of our industry. For too long our marketing procedures have resulted in Canadian exporters going abroad and saying: "This is the product we have; are you interested?" That as opposed to going abroad, identifying the needs for forest products, coming back to Canada and creating those products to meet specific market demands. That would be a major step forward for many producers in our country. In other words, identify the markets more precisely and take advantage of them, and perhaps become more aggressive in seeking out those markets. Also, a great deal can be done through the federal Government to assist our export sector and assure the necessary financial support so we can compete with some of our major competitors.
The Hon. Member mentioned productivity. When you look at countries with which we compete, western European countries and some of the American countries, one of the things they have in place that we do not is what I will refer to as industrial democracy. They have recognized that by involving all employees in their operation, be it large or small, in a
Supply
meaningful way, their ability to be competitive is that much greater.
As a first step in this direction, and I emphasize only a first step, I suggest that something like the profit-sharing schemes we have seen in certain corporations ought to be looked at in Canada. The United States has over 400,000 profit-sharing schemes; we have approximately 2,000. In other words, we are abysmally behind even the U.S., let alone our western European competitors who are miles ahead of us, not only in profit sharing but in the whole area of involving employees in a responsible way through profit sharing, responsibility sharing and information sharing.
When we begin to democratize the workplace and involve all employees in the productive capacity of our plants, then we will see our competitive advantage increase substantially. However, while we maintain the old-fashioned, neanderthal approach of bosses and workers, we will continue to have difficulties as we act in a mode which was perhaps more appropriate in the 1920s but which has no place whatsoever in the labour management world of the 1980s, let alone the 1990s.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to address a question to the Hon. Member having to do with the fact that in British Columbia at the present time much of our forest land is being devastated by insect attacks. In his riding there is a problem with the tussock moth and Douglas fir trees. Can he comment on what is being done about that? I think there was a virus they were going to use and there was a problem getting it licensed. Perhaps he could give us some information on that program.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, the tussock moth was a major problem in the forests of central British Columbia. The solution was brought to my attention by a number of people involved in entomology who said that the virus was really the only solution. It had some problems but it was the most obvious solution. I brought that to the attention of various officials in Ottawa whose approval was required for its application. I must say they took some extraordinary steps to provide intermediate approval to allow this to proceed, but because of the unavailability in Canada of an adequate source, nothing very much was accomplished.
What that proved to me was that while the bureaucrats were quite conscious of the problem and aware of the solution, they lacked any sort of comprehensive plan and were acting on their own individual initiative. With inadequate funding and a lack of any long-term plan, they were really unable to respond to this mini-crisis in central British Columbia. So rather than politicians planning three or four years in advance, we need to look at it over 40 to 60-year intervals, the time it takes to grow a mature tree.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today raises a number of fundamental questions. It is couched in the language that is customary around here and which may come as a surprise to onlookers and watchers on TV, namely the phraseology of Government failure to take action. Of course, I do not agree with that kind of approach and terminology because, as we all know, in particular in relation to the development of resource industries, there has been a lot of government action, a lot of activity and a lot of taxpayers' funds which have been put into the development of our natural resources over the past decade.
I would conclude, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a question of failure here. The Hon. Member in his motion is putting a basic, fundamental issue on the floor for debate today for a critical analysis on the part of all concerned individuals and Members of this House. In that respect he is doing everybody
a great service by allowing us to look at this issue in a partisan way, and at the same time I hope in a constructive way.
If there is trouble in our resource industries, 1 would be inclined to think it is because we have had a slowdown in the economy, some very serious downturns in certain aspects of the economy. There has been a very serious drop in demand which has affected the prices of our natural resources, particularly in mining and the lumber industry. Certainly to attribute the behaviour of economists in the world to inaction by the Government is not just stretching it too far, but is pointing the finger in the wrong direction.
Over the years this Government, as colleagues will subsequently demonstrate, has shown an enormous sense of awareness of and sensitivity to our interests in natural resources. As some of the speakers have already indicated, our natural resources represent a substantial form of income for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. They represent jobs in very large numbers and therefore are a substantial part of our Gross National Product and of the wealth that we all share and benefit from.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I will attempt very briefly to outline our position on the question of forestry which is very close to our minds and hearts. This House has been made familiar, on a number of occasions since the beginning of the life of this particular Parliament, with our concern for forestry. We have given the Canadian Forestry Service higher status by identifying the person at the top of it with the title of an Assistant Deputy Minister, who was also given at the same time the assignment of preparing, in conjunction with my predecessor, a strategy.
My predecessor released the strategy in 1981 which summarized the problems which are facing forestry in Canada, and also outlined a plan for action. The strategy has its foundation in a national forest policy based on co-operation with the provincial Governments. We recognize ownership on the part of the Provinces of this resource and we realize that there must not be a pulling apart or a moving at cross-purposes between the provincial and federal Governments in this particular field of resources. Rather we must work together and we must both work with industry and unions as well.
As a result, this policy which the federal Government is pursuing is one which rests on co-operation with the Provinces. In this regard we have utilized the forum of the Canadian Council of Resources and Environment Ministers as well as held bilateral discussions with provincial Governments. The forest sector strategy pointed out that, in effect, the virgin forests have been mined and little thought has been given in the past to future crops. We must focus our attention therefore on farming and managing properly the forests and on emphasizing intensive forest management and forest renewal.
Not only must we do this, Mr. Speaker, we must also address problems that we recognized, including the need to protect our forests from fire, insects and disease, to encourage the management of private woodlots, to increase the management of the forests on Indian reserves, to fill the need for
November 21, 1983

professional foresters, and to foster the important area of forest research necessary for all of these objectives.
The role and involvement of the federal Government in forestry is basic to the health of the sector. The federal Government is committed to forestry and will continue to act in its support in concert and co-operation with the Provinces. It has indeed been on this basis that we have been able to achieve a series of accomplishments initiated by my predecessors which 1 hope to continue and build upon. As the first step we felt it necessary, prior to the implementation to the forest sector strategy, to establish a national system for the collection, analysis and dissemination of forestry data in furtherance of intensive forestry management policies, planning and programs. This work is being conducted as a component of the Petawawa National Forestry Institute. Financial resources approved for this program for the period of 1981-82 to 198384 amount to some $5.7 million. It has enabled us to produce the 1981 Canada forest inventory as a basic step.
Responding to the challenges of forest management and renewal, and in the spirit of co-operation, we have committed ourselves to enter into agreement with each of the Provinces in support of programs to meet the reforestation needs of the forest sector. Two agreements have already been signed, one with Nova Scotia of August of 1982 which provides some $30 million of federal funds over five years. A significant program of aid to private woodlot owners is built into this agreement. An agreement with Prince Edward Island was signed in July of this year which allows for federal funds of some $15 million over five years.
In the case of Newfoundland funds have been provided to enhance the existing agreement totalling some $16 million over three years for employment stimulation. I hope that we will soon be able to announce a new agreement with Manitoba. Another agreement is being put into motion with Saskatchewan and with Alberta. Negotiations are well underway with Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and British Columbia. These Provinces are currently under agreements arranged by DREE which expire in March of 1984. I would like particularly to bring to the attention of the NDP critic and the Progressive Conservative Party that the agreements which are now in place total some $400 million over the five past years alone.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Forestry Service also prepared a private woodlot development policy. It provides the basis for private woodlot programs in federal-provincial forest agreements. Earlier this year, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) announced the plan for the development of the Gaspe Bas-St. Laurent region. In the program some $19 million will be devoted to assistance to the Groupement Fores-tier for private woodlot management.
All of these agreements, Mr. Speaker, are based on the Government's policy that is tuned in to and focuses on forest renewal. This policy requires a financial commitment on the part of the federal Government and an even larger amount by the Provinces and by industry. It remains to be seen whether all levels will be able to find these funds in times of fiscal restraint.
Supply
Given the high unemployment in the forest sector, we began a job-creation program last year using Section 38 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Canadian Forestry Service was provided with $34 million to top up the benefits of unemployment insurance receipts under this program. As I said last Friday, this totalled as a combined amount some $140 million. To date, this has provided 14,000 positions, representing a quarter of a million weeks of employment.
The program was particularly successful in British Columbia where it was known as EBAP, the Employment Bridging Assistance Program. Unfortunately, in June of this year the Province of British Columbia decided to curtail its involvement in this program, sharply reducing its effectiveness. However, the federal Government is continuing this initiative under the new Canada Works Program. We are hopeful that industry and the Provinces will generate sufficient projects to allow us to make a substantial contribution to our forestry renewal objectives with these funds.
The federal Government has historically provided Canada with its basic forestry research and development. This has been done by the Canadian Forestry Service with support from sister organizations such as the Forintek Canada Corporation. The forest sector strategy recognized the situation of underfunding to this institution and is moving in that direction.
The House may recall that Cabinet approved the research and development component for the strategy and provided some $5.5 million to the Canadian Forestry Service for research and development for this fiscal year. The R and D component calls for a substantial increase in funding for subsequent years, including basic support for Forintek to maintain our competitive position for forest products and lead us to forest renewal as called for in the strategy.
In addition to that, however, funds have already been committed to the expansion and upgrading of Canadian Forestry Service research labs across the country, including some $14 million for the expansion of the Pacific Forestry Research Centre in Victoria, some $13 million for an addition to the Great Lakes Forestry Research Centre in the Soo, some $10.5 million for additions to the Laurentian Forestry Research Centre in Ste. Foy and some $22.5 million for a new Mari-times Forestry Research Centre in Fredericton. Also some $17 million has been provided for the expansion of pulp and paper research facilities in Victoria and Pointe Claire.
As part of the Maritime forestry complex in Fredericton, the Government is providing over $10 million for a Maritime forest ranger school. Also in keeping with the spirit of co-operation with the provincial Governments, we have signed a memorandum of understanding with the Provinces on the co-ordination of forestry research.
I am sure that Members of the House are in part familiar with the activities in support of the control of forest fires which have cost Canada as much wood as is harvested in certain years. The CL-215 water bomber program will contribute significantly to our efforts in fighting forest fires. I believe this

November 21, 1983
Supply
has been a major illustration of co-operation with the Provinces in response to a major problem. Through joint arrangements with the Provinces, we are purchasing some 29 water bombers from Canadair, of which 17 will be owned by the federal Government, four to be used exclusively by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for use north of 60. The entire fleet will be co-ordinated by the Interagency Forestry Centre in Winnipeg which is, in itself, a very good example of federal-provincial co-operation in forestry methods.
Let me say a few words on our forestry initiatives on Indian reserves. I agree with the mover of the motion that the forests on Indian lands have been neglected in the past. It is understood that this resource could provide twice the benefits to the Indian people that it currently provides. We have been recently working in close co-operation with my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), to develop a comprehensive program of Indian forest land management. A working group of officials from the Canadian Forestry Service and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been set up for this very purpose. What is significant, however, is that this working group is headed by representatives of the Assembly of First Nations.
The basic objectives and principles of this program are that it will provide for economic, social, cultural, spiritual and environmental benefits for the Indian people through the wise management of forest resources on Indian lands. It will be controlled and administered by the Indian people and implemented at the community or band level. This approach is entirely consistent with the recommendations of the House of Commons Special Committee on Indian Self-Government. Within the context of Indian ownership of India resources and in the control of Indian development, the objectives of the proposed program are: to increase the number of hectares of productive Indian forest land; to increase the sustainable annual harvest on Indian lands; to increase the number of Indian persons productively employed in all aspects of the forestry sector; to increase the number of Indian enterprises actively engaged in direct and indirect viable forestry and forestry-related activities; and finally, to develop the technical, operational and managerial skills of Indian people consistent with the requirements for an economically viable Indian forestry sector.
The financial support for this program will come from several sources and the Canadian Forestry Service will provide the necessary technical and scientific expertise. We are now taking an excellent opportunity for the federal Government to establish a useful and rewarding program in co-operation with the Indian people.
Turning to human resources, it is indeed a potential problem for the future but we have anticipated well what may happen and have taken steps to address it. The human resources development component of the sector strategy addressed this concern and we have been able to provide over $15 million to expand the pool of professional forestry manpower. This
money will provide for forestry scholarships, contract research and development and summer student employment to some 300 students per year. Most of this money will go to Canadian universities and particularly to the six forestry schools across the country, the University of British Columbia, the University of Alberta, Lakehead University, the University of Toronto, Universite Laval and the University of New Brunswick.
Another area of increased federal activity in response to the forest sector strategy is in international trade. In recent years there has been a successful program of overseas market development of British Columbia forest products under agreement between the federal Government, the Province and the British Columbia Council of Forest Industries. This program will be expanded to other Provinces and negotiations are under way to do so by my colleague, the Minister responsible for DRIE.
An important issue to forestry is the use of pesticides and insecticides. Pesticides are designed to kill organisms that cause environmental disease, insects and weeds. By their very nature, pesticides are toxic and have the potential for adverse effects on non-target life. Management of pesticides requires weighing risks and benefits on the basis of value judgments, including economic and social factors. There is public dissatisfaction with the current management system from both the environmental protection and research development perspectives.
I suggest that two major issues emerge from the analysis of pesticides management. One is the lack of public confidence. Contributing factors to this lack of confidence include confidential information, shifting burden of proof, little public access to the decision points, uncertainty of risk assessments and conflict of interest between environmental protection and resource development.
The second issue is the public concern extending from immediate human health to long-range environmental quality. There are multiple jurisdictions involved, including federal, provincial and municipal, which complicates this issue.
A great deal must be done to improve this situation. For its part, in improving the situation for the forest sector, the Canadian Forestry Service is developing effective and environmentally acceptable materials and methods to respond to the needs of the forest manager and is developing biological and non-chemical methods and means for forest pest management.
I see you are impatient with me, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude briefly. In summary, much has been accomplished since the preparation of the forest sector strategy for Canada, including increased support to forestry schools, expanded forestry research facilities, the development of a national water bomber fleet, forestry job-creation projects and an expanded overseas trade program. There remain two major priorities: increased research and development and the major task of forest renewal. Research and development is essential to protect our forests from threatening insects, disease and fire.

As 1 was saying, research and development is essential to protect our forests from threatening insects, des-ease and fire, to develop faster growing species, to develop means of managing forest productivity from a shrinking land resource base. The Canadian Forestry Service requires a substantial increase in resources to do its work. A major investment in forest renewal is required by the Provinces, industry and the federal Government to ensure an adequate supply of wood in order to sustain and enhance the forest industry which remains Canada's largest employer.
The evidence is clear: failure to act will jeopardize the 300 or more single industry, forestry-based communities and critically affect our balance of trade. The investments are labour intensive and give employment, particularly to our young people and our native people. However, in times of tight fiscal restraint and low profits for industry, the tendency is for us to postpone these essential tasks. Industry and Provinces must also confirm their resolve to rebuild our forests to ensure that future generations benefit as we are benefiting today.
Can we save Canadian forestry, it has been asked. The plan to do so is there. It has been supported and endorsed by various organizations, including the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, by the Canadian Forest Advisory Council, the Forestry Industry Advisory Committee, industry associations, professional institutes of foresters and by all Parties of this House. The policies and plans are being implemented and the decisions are also being made.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have a couple of questions for the Minister which I think are pertinent to the debate. In the Minister's final comments he admitted what we have suspected all along, namely that there are tendencies by both federal and provincial Governments to postpone what the Minister called the major effort that must be made to save our forests. Since the Minister is approaching a critical deadline this Thursday when there is the annual auction to redistribute money that has not been used, and knowing that the Minister is behind in his commitment to come up with this $130 million for forest renewal, is the forest renewal side, which the Minister thinks to be critical, one of the things he has a tendency to recommend postponement of, or is the Minister confident that on Thursday he will get the necessary funds to meet the commitments he has made to the whole forest community?
Second, knowing of the tragedy, that of the resignation of the Assistant Deputy Minister and knowing of the invaluable contribution Mr. Reed has made in the effort to rebuild against all possible odds a federal forestry service, what is the Government's plan to replace Mr. Reed? Also, what is the next stage of the upgrading of the forest service? Is it to

appoint a deputy minister? As the Minister well knows, and I am sure he agrees with me, the environmental side of his portfolio is overshadowing and taking precedence over some of his other responsibilities. 1 give the Minister credit: his heart is in the right place but he has the responsibility of a dual portfolio. Unfortunately, bureaucrats on the one side are overshadowing his responsibility on the forest side. I would appreciate the Minister responding to these questions.

Mr. Speaker, I will try. Both are very difficult questions. The first relates to a decision to be made next Thursday. I cannot anticipate the answer because 1 lack the ability of a clairvoyant to know what the outcome will be. If the Hon. Member wants to know from me, as he did last Friday, whether 1 will put into the cause of forestry all my energy and commitment, my answer is definitely yes. 1 hope we will eventually find the funds required for the implementation of this policy, keeping in mind, as 1 mentioned earlier, that this is a joint kind of effort and that the Provinces will also have to indicate that they, too, put forestry at the top of their priorities in the selection of priorities which they have themselves. That it be recognized by the Provinces is extremely important since, after all, they own some 90 per cent of Crown lands.
As to the departure of the Assistant Deputy Minister, it is a great loss but not a tragedy because the departure was the wish of the official himself. He came to Ottawa with the intention of filling the position for three years and his three-year tenure expired at the end of October. It is a position that will be very difficult to fill by someone else with the same commitment and dynamic drive that Les Reed demonstrated during his three years. He has left with us a very important legacy. We are, however, in the process of looking for potential candidates willing to fill the position.
As to the final half of the Hon. Member's second question, 1 do not see, in all frankness and having been in the Department for only three months, a situation whereby the Canadian Forestry Service is overshadowed by other sections in the Department. 1 think it has all the scope and its place in the sun, as have other interests in Environment Canada. Certainly as long as I am in this portfolio it will have my ear and fullest attention.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister. In all modesty the Minister has not mentioned his qualifications. 1 would point out to the House and to the people that the Minister is a professional forester. He is to be commended.
The Minister mentioned in his remarks the very substantial amount of $400 million which was DRIE money. That money will certainly not all be channelled through forestry even over a five-year period, which would amount to $125 million a year because the budget of DRIE in the past has been $600 million or $700 million in total a year.
One other thing. Since he wears the hat of the Minister of the Environment, I must tell him 1 am concerned and greatly interested in the acid rain problem. We on the committee, and I think the Minister as well, are aware of the possibility of

grave injury to reforestation, to the small seedlings coming up. I hope his Department is giving top priority to that as well.

Dealing with the second point first, Mr. Speaker, the answer is definitely yes. We are devoting all possible attention to the long-term impact of acid rain on forest growth. The scientific data on this continent is very recent and young. However, there is enough evidence in Europe to make a strong case about the serious damage and effect of acid rain not only on seedlings but on grown-up stands. This is the kind of persuasive message which I have to bring to our American friends whenever I meet with them on environmental issues, particularly on acid rain, in Washington, Indianapolis or in New York.
1 report with regret to the Hon. Member that the operation of convincing our friends to the south is not an easy one because in some quarters they are still looking for scientific evidence to prove the point the Hon. Member made so eloquently a moment ago. This is very serious because we are talking about long-term damage for which there is already evidence in Scandinavia and Central Europe. While I can assure him that we are paying a lot of attention to the consequences of acid rain on the growth of existing stands, 1 also report to him the fact that we are still in the phase of trying to convince certain quarters south of the border. My counterpart in Washington, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, is having an absolutely miserable and difficult time convincing his own administration that this issue deserves attention in order to reduce damage to American forests themselves. It has now reached a point where unless there is clear indication of leadership on the part of the American government, we will be engaging in this debate for a long, long time.

for forestry agree to consult with his counterparts in that Province to see if there are any ways or means which can be found to alleviate the pressure and to have the Ministers responsible in that Province through their Premier agree to some alleviation of pressure by reducing power rates for that plant at this time?

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to speak this morning on the motion brought forward by the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). Normally the only time we get to talk about resources in this House is when the Government comes forward with a new proposal for yet more tax burdens on a resource industry or comes in to nationalize an industry either through the back door or front door.
My intention this morning is not to examine any one resource industry. We were pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River indicating the importance of various industries. However, my intention is to examine the reasons for the failure of this Government's policies in these areas, the philosophy that it maintains and its ideas which have given rise to the failure of forestry, mining and other resource industries.
Supply
Before 1 get into that, 1 would like to preface my remarks with a couple of observations. The first observation that is apparent to almost every Canadian is that we are the most resource-rich nation in the world, especially when you take relative populations into account.
The whole history of Canada, or a very great part of it, deals with the development, exploitation and utilization of the natural resources of this country. It was in the sixteenth century that fishermen from European ports, Portugal, Spain and other countries, first came over in small vessels to exploit the riches of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the fur trade blossomed. It was probably the most important industry in New France. The fur trade helped to develop the rest of the hinterland outside of that small area in the St. Lawrence Valley. The fur traders went far afield and penetrated into the vast interior.
1 was fortunate to receive just the other day a publication by the Fur Council of Canada entitled "The Fur Industry in Canada". It gives us a description of the proud history of the fur trade. It is sad to relate that at the present time the fur industry is under something of an attack. The trappers have been faced with inequities in taxation and are finding it tough to survive. An even greater threat to that industry are certain people who do not like to see fur-bearing animals taken in Canada. It is incumbent upon this House to protect the trapping industry.
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries we got under way with the exploitation of our forest resources and agriculture, especially western Canadian agriculture potential. There was a taking up of agricultural lands in western Canada. The forests of eastern Canada, especially in the time of the continental policies of Napoleon with regard to the timber industry of New Brunswick, first came into being.
In the twentieth century, Canada and Canadian resources have really come into their own. We have had the development of mines. Around the 1940s we had development starting in the oil and gas industry, especially in western Canada. That industry is now finding new worlds to conquer offshore in eastern Canada and in the Arctic. In this century we have developed hydro-electric resources. There is more to come, of that I have no doubt.
It is interesting that we have to take into account that a lot of our natural resources can only be developed and exploited if we have the knowledge available so to do. We must have the capital available to develop them and find people who are skilled in the exploitation of resources. For these reasons, we on this side are most concerned with the continuation of research and development in this country on natural resource issues and the training of personnel.
With all our resources, Canada ought to be the richest nation on the face of the earth. In fact, in the fifties and sixties it looked like we were getting there. We were second only to the United States in standard of living throughout the world.
That brings me to my second undeniable observation, that since the present Government under the Prime Minister (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
November 21, 1983
Supply
Trudeau) took office in 1968, everything has slid downhill. We are now no longer second in standard of living of the world but fourteenth, fifteenth or sixteenth. We have slid downhill. The underlying reason for this is that we have neglected our resource industries and those who work and invest in our resource industries, those whose livelihood depends on the forests, mines, agriculture and fishing. Had we husbanded our resources and adopted policies conducive to their continued development, we would not be fifteenth in the standard of living table in the world. We would be first, where we deserve to be and by rights should be.
Let us look at the over-all policies and the reasons Members opposite have failed to increase the Canadian standard of living but have allowed it to decline, and the reason there has been failure of resource industry policy. The first reason has to be that hon. gentlemen opposite-a bunch of academics, professional politicians, people with an administrative background-have had little experience in the outside world. Gentlemen opposite have not been involved with industrial organizations. They do not come from areas where resource industries are of fundamental importance. They are more interested in philosophical ideas, particularly in changing the way of thinking of people. They love to do that to Canadians. They want everyone to think a certain way. They engage in advertising and everything else in order to get people to think their way rather than concentrate on practical, economic issues.
For example, for two years this House was preoccupied with the constitutional issue. It was a manufactured issue. I did not come across a farmer, miner or logger three or four years ago who had that at the top of his list of priorities. There was nothing wrong with the Constitution we had before, yet we spent two years, to the exclusion of almost everything else, talking about a Constitution when we should have been talking about getting the economy of Canada back on track.
Gentlemen opposite are imbued with these socialist ideas. They think that the state should control and regulate every aspect of the economy and other areas of life throughout Canada. They think that as the Government they can direct everything that goes on in the country. It does not work. Instead of having one huge pyramid with the Prime Minister and the Cabinet at the top, giving direction to and regulating everything that goes on in Canadian life, there should be a series of pyramids. Much of industry should be fairly independent of Government. The Government should give only the most general direction. Industry should be relatively independent. Universities and education facilities should be independent. As well, the artistic community should be independent and we should have these independent societies operating together rather than having everything directed by the Government.
We see that the Government is using its direct influence to get into the resource industries. An example of this, of course, is Petro-Canada. I cannot see one good reason why we need a
nationalized oil industry in Canada, without which we were doing far better. What has happened is that the Government has taxed every gallon of gasoline and heating oil that Canadians buy in order to fulfil its socialist ideals.
The situation with Petro-Canada is bad enough. It was only recently that, through the use of closure, the Canagrex Bill was forced through the House of Commons. The Government's intention for Canagrex is clear. It wants to get a stranglehold grip on agriculture in Canada, which is another area that ought to be independent.
Socialist views have come to the forefront with Bill C-48 and its back-in provisions. If someone acquires some land and drills an oil well or a gas well in what the Government calls Canadian lands but what I call territorial lands and risks his own money to find something that looks profitable, along comes the friendly Government of Canada, through Petro-Canada, saying: "Okay, we are going to take over 25 per cent of this venture". I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if this is the way to encourage enterprise in the nation.
The Government has the idea that all resources belong to the state and that anyone who gets into the resource exploitation or development industry is entitled only to what is called an economic rent. That means that the investor takes his risk, spends his money, devotes his time and energy to something, and if it does prove to be successful, somebody from the Government of Canada will come along and say: "We figure that you should get 7 per cent on your investment and that is all you are going to get. We are going to take every other nickel that you make and put it into our coffers because the state owns the resources."
This concept is evident in the progressive incremental royalties that apply to oil and gas exploitation on federal lands under Bill C-48. Unfortunately, this concept is now so pervasive throughout Canadian government, not only the federal Government but provincial Governments as well, that it goes almost unchallenged. I can tell you that the concept of the state owning all of the resources is wrong. Resources should belong to the finders of those resources and the people who have worked to make a go of them.
In the case of minerals and oil and gas, the people who find the ore deposits or the oil and gas on Crown lands should become the owners of those resources and deposits. If a fisherman were to find a new area for fishing, he should be entitled to extraordinary profits from developing that new area. I am ashamed to think of what is happening within the Department of Fisheries in Winnipeg where officials are trying to use the same concept of economic rent on fisheries. A fisherman will be entitled to make so much money a year and no more. If he makes more than that amount of money, the Government will take it all back or tell him to stop fishing because he has been too successful.
In the case of farms and agricultural operations, the concept is not so much one of the resource belonging to the person who finds that resource but rather one of the persons who puts the effort into breaking the sod where it has never been broken before and building up something which will be a part of
November 21, 1983

Canada becoming the owner of that resource. In exchange for doing that, that farmer or agriculturalist should be entitled to ownership in the resource, which in this case is agricultural land. That is the concept that existed when the western Canadian Prairies were settled. I think we must get back to that way of thinking rather than the concept of the state owning everything and perhaps allowing a little bit of farming, a little bit of mining and a little bit of fishing to take place while saying: "Do not by any means make any profit out of those ventures because, if you do, we will take it all back in the form of taxes and royalties".
We on this side of the House agree that resource exploitation should be subject to taxation. I am not saying that there should be no taxes on mines, farms and oil fields. However, these taxes should not be designed to skim everything off the top and leave nothing. In cases where some people are eminently successful and come up with a greatly profitable venture, those people should be and deserve to be highly rewarded. It is necessary that some people be successful and rewarded in order that their success act as an incentive for others to do the same, to risk money in prospecting ventures and to risk hard work in developing agricultural lands.
Last, Sir, we recognize that Members opposite, especially those on the Treasury benches, are by and large people from the central metropolitan areas of Canada. They do not have a first-hand knowledge of the resource industry and they do not have a feeling for the resource industry. The fact is that enterprise in Canada is by and large to be found in the extremities of the country. The core, Sir, has a tendency to grow soft. Ideas that result in the exploitation of the hinterland of Canada where those resources are located and result in that money and wealth and power being brought into the central area of Canada find favour with the present Government.
In the few moments left before one o'clock, I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, an editorial in the October 13 edition of The Northern Miner. That editorial contrasts the $275 million combined grant put up by the federal and Quebec Governments to build a helicopter plant in Montreal, which admittedly is to create some 3,700 jobs over 20 years, with the gold mining developments in the Hemlo area of Ontario. It is expected that as a result of new gold finds in that area, some 5,000 to 8,000 people will move there and the direct number of jobs created will be very much equivalent to those created by the so-called investment of some $275 million of taxpayers' money in Montreal. However, the big difference is that in the Hemlo area, the situation was all brought about by private investment. Not one dollar of taxpayers' money was expended. What will happen is that that privately developed area will be taxed in order to provide funds for the helicopter plant in Montreal.
This is the approach that is taken by the Government. The Government will not allow economic developments to occur naturally according to market conditions in Canada. It insists that it has the responsibility to redirect funds into the areas in which it can mine for votes.
I see that it is rapidly approaching one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps you would be kind enough to allow me to call it one o'clock.
